To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1. chimpanzee brain responses to vocal stimuli are similar to those of humans and monkeys; 2. chimpanzee brain event-related potential measures are similar to those obtained in humans under passive experimental conditions; 3. chimpanzee responses to adaptively relevant conspecific vocal stimuli are right hemisphere lateralized, whereas responses to a rare stimulus under passive conditions are not lateralized; and 4. chimpanzee brain measures of vocal perception show ontogenetic changes similar to those observed in human infants

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chimpanzee ERPs show a similar pattern to humans, with some interesting differences.
chimpanzees are capable of perceiving and responding to vocal stimuli in the same way that humans do.
chimpanzees, like humans and other primates, have the capacity for the perception of vocal stimuli, but that their perceptual capacities are not as advanced.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ontogeny, and to a certain extent the phylogeny, of vocal perception is similar to humans and monkeys.
the chimpanzees' brain responds to conspecific vocal stimuli in a way very similar to that reported for the human brain, and in a way different from that of other primates.

chimpanzee auditory perception is similar to human and nonhuman primate auditory perception in the early stages, but chimpanzees may differ in their later processing of auditory information, especially in the context of vocal communication.
The main takeaway from our work is that
chimpanzees are able to process conspecific and human calls in a manner similar to humans, and that the processing of these calls involves similar brain regions and cognitive processes.
chimpanzees, as with humans, can show enhanced ERP responses to conspecific and human affective vocalizations, and that these responses are right hemisphere lateralized.
chimpanzees, like humans, can discriminate between vocalizations and other sounds, and that they show a similar ERP response to the rare stimulus.
